title: Give the Bots the Clicks. Keep the Decisions.
originalityNote: Same topic and promise as the source (build AI agents for every part of life), rebuilt by the viewer's day instead of the source's product walkthrough: hook on measured time-use data, define the agent, the routing mechanism, a worked example with labelled hypothetical hours, life bots, team bots, Goldratt's constraint method, a money bot with a hard no-move rule, honest risks and a human line, and a first-week plan. All personal figures from the source are cut; every number is verified at Microsoft, McKinsey, xAI, or Goldratt, or labelled hypothetical. No creator is named, no video is cited.

sources.title: Microsoft, 2023 Work Trend Index: Will AI Fix Work?
McKinsey Global Institute, Capturing business value with social technologies, November 2012
Goldratt, The Goal (1984) - five focusing steps, as quoted in Reference for Business

scenes.beat: Hook: the week that isn't work
scenes.narration: You open your inbox at nine, and by noon you have answered mail for three hours and done nothing that was yours. That's not a bad morning. That's the job now, and it's been the job for years. In twenty twenty three, the average person spent fifty seven percent of the time inside their work apps just communicating. Forty three percent went to creating. So more than half your week isn't work. It's work about work. Ask yourself what you did yesterday that only you could do. Then ask what a bot could have done. This video hands that half to bots, and keeps the decisions with you.

claims.text: The average person spends 57% of time in Microsoft 365 communicating and only 43% creating.
claims.sourceQuote: Of time spent in Microsoft 365, the average person spends 57% communicating and only 43% creating.

scenes.narration: First, the difference. A chatbot answers your question. An agent does the job. You give it a job, it signs into your tools, and it comes back when it needs a decision. That's the whole difference. The tool this runs on is called Grok Bot. Each bot gets its own computer in the cloud, and it keeps working when your laptop is shut. One account shares one computer, so the bots pass work between themselves in the same thread. It starts at thirty dollars a month. Check it before you buy, because it changes. Show it a workflow once, and it saves the steps as a routine it runs on its own next time. Usage comes from a weekly pool, so a bot that runs all day costs more than a bot that checks in twice. Start small and watch the meter. That's why the setup below is three moves, not thirty. One bot in charge, and a few bots with one job each. The handoff rule ties them together.

scenes.narration: Back in twenty twelve, knowledge workers spent twenty eight percent of each day on email. Thirteen hours a week. Searching for information takes nineteen percent. Talking inside the company takes fourteen. The actual job takes thirty nine. Sixty four percent of employees say they don't have enough time and energy to get their work done. That's the first thing to hand over. Not the thinking. The sorting, the filing, the first draft of the reply.
